unit.unitTitle: Better, Worse, and What I Have To Do
unit.unitOverview: Compare two choices and say which one is more useful. Say how a thing is done: more slowly, the most carefully. Say what you have to do, and what might happen. Point at one person or one thing: the woman who fixed it.
unit.learningPath:
The lesson: listen, repeat and say it.
Words: listen, look and say. 28 words.
Patterns: 4 cards. Read the one done for you first.
Reading: read 3 texts and answer the questions.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, then listen back.
Writing: 4 short texts. Made-up answers are OK.
Practice: 6 exercises. Check with the answers.
Quiz: 12 questions. Five look back at Units 1 to 6.

visual.lectureScript:
Hello. This is Unit 7.
It is the last unit of this part of the course.
In this unit you choose between two things.
You say what you have to do about your choice.
And you say what is only possible.
First, comparing.
You already know the short words.
Cheap, cheaper, the cheapest.
Now the longer words. Listen.
Use-ful. Two parts.
A word with two parts or more does not take -er.
It takes more.
This map is more useful than that list.
Care-ful. Two parts. More careful.
She is more careful with money than I am.
For three or more things, say the most.
Of the four bags, this one is the most useful.
Say the before most.
The most useful. Not just most useful.
Now, how a thing is done.
You know these words: slowly, carefully, clearly, easily.
They end in -ly. They say how.
To compare them, say more.
Please speak more slowly.
He drives more carefully than his sister.
For three or more, say the most.
Of the three of us, she reads the most clearly.
Careful is the person. Carefully is the way.
Now, rules.
Have to means you cannot avoid it.
The notice says members only.
I have to show my card.
He, she and it take has to.
She has to work on Saturday.
Yesterday, it is had to.
The bus did not come, so I had to walk.
The question is: Do I have to pay today?
The answer can be: No, you do not have to.
Listen to that again. Do not have to.
It does not mean no.
It means there is no rule about it.
Now, what is only possible.
Might, may and could.
It might rain later.
I may be late.
She could be at the desk.
No -s, and no to.
It might rain. Not: it might to rain.
Last, saying exactly which one.
Two short sentences.
The woman fixed my phone. She works here.
Put them together with who.
The woman who fixed my phone works here.
Who is for a person.
Which is for a thing.
I lost the card which opens the door.
That works for both.
This is the form that you have to sign.
Where is for a place.
This is the room where you wait.
Take out the extra she or it.
Not: the woman who she fixed my phone.
One more thing. This unit is a checkpoint.
It closes Stage 4.
Five quiz questions look back at Units 1 to 6.
So read the cards, do the practice, and check every answer.
Now go to the words. See you at the quiz.

readings.passageScript:
Lena: Look at these two English courses. Which one do you choose?
Omar: Course A costs 80. Course B costs 120. What is the difference?

Omar: So course B is more useful, but it costs more.

readings.title: One Word, a Whole Family
readings.setting: A page from a study guide about word endings.
readings.passageScript:
Many English words grow from one small word.
Take the word care. Add -ful and you get careful: you give it your attention.
Add -less and you get careless: you do not.
Add -ly and you get carefully. That one says how you do a thing.
Now take the word use. Useful means it helps you. Useless means it does not help at all.
The endings do the same work on other small words.
Help becomes helpful. Harm becomes harmful. Pain becomes painful.
So -ful often means full of that thing, and -less often means without it.
This is useful when you meet a new word on a form or a notice.
You do not need a dictionary every time.
Find the small word inside, then look at the ending.
In my view, this is the fastest way to grow your English.
Be careful, though. Not every word takes both endings.
We say helpful and helpless. We say useful and useless.
But there is no word kindless. When you are not sure, check the word.

STUDY ROOM
This notice is an example for your English practice. Rules where you live may be different.
Open: Monday to Saturday, 9 in the morning to 8 at night.
1. Members only. You have to show your card at the desk.

grammar.title: More useful, the most careful
grammar.explanation:
A short word takes -er and the -est: cheap, cheaper, the cheapest.
A longer word does not. It takes more and the most.
Use-ful has two parts, so it is more useful.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Longer words take more and the most:
useful, more useful, the most useful
careful, more careful, the most careful
helpful, more helpful, the most helpful
difficult, more difficult, the most difficult
expensive, more expensive, the most expensive

Two things. Say than after more:
This map is more useful than that list.

Three or more things. Say the before most:
Of the four bags, this one is the most useful.

Short words still take -er and the -est:
cheap, cheaper, the cheapest
safe, safer, the safest

Good and bad do not follow this at all:
good, better, the best
bad, worse, the worst
grammar.workedExample:
Two courses. Course A gives a book. Course B gives a book and ten lessons.
1. Which word do I want? Useful.
2. Count the parts: use-ful. Two parts.
3. Two parts, so I use more, not -er.
4. Course B is more useful than course A.
5. Now a third one. Course C gives twenty lessons.
6. Three things, so I use the most.
7. Course C is the most useful of the three.
8. Check: I wrote the before most.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to use more and -er together.
No: This map is more usefuller.
Yes: This map is more useful.
It is easy to leave out the before most.
No: This one is most helpful.
Yes: This one is the most helpful.
grammar.memoryTip: One part, add -er. Two parts or more, say more.

6. This road is ___ than that road. (safe)
7. Sun in the afternoon is ___ than sun in the morning. (harmful)

grammar.answerKey:

grammar.title: More slowly, the most carefully
grammar.explanation:
You know the -ly words: slowly, carefully, clearly, easily.
They say how a thing is done.
To compare them, say more. To pick one out of three, say the most.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
How a thing is done:
slowly, more slowly, the most slowly
carefully, more carefully, the most carefully
clearly, more clearly, the most clearly
easily, more easily, the most easily
quickly, more quickly, the most quickly

Two people:
She types more quickly than I do.
Please speak more slowly.

Three or more:
Of the three of us, he works the most carefully.

The -ly word comes after the verb:
He drives carefully. He drives more carefully than his sister.

Careful is the person. Carefully is the way:
She is a careful driver. She drives carefully.
grammar.workedExample:
Two people fill in the same form. One makes no mistake. One makes four.
1. I am talking about how they do it, so I need a -ly word: carefully.
2. I am comparing two people, so I use more.
3. The first person fills in the form more carefully than the second.
4. Now a third person. She makes no mistake and she checks it twice.
5. Three people, so I use the most.
6. Of the three, she fills in the form the most carefully.
7. Check: the word ends in -ly, and it comes after the verb.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to use the describing word instead of the -ly word.
No: She works more careful than me.
Yes: She works more carefully than me.
It is easy to add -er to a -ly word.
No: Please speak slowlier.
Yes: Please speak more slowly.
grammar.memoryTip: The person is careful. The way is carefully. To compare the way, say more.
grammar.practice:

3. He drives ___ than his sister. (carefully)
4. I can read the new notice ___ than the old one. (easily)
5. Of all the people here, he answers ___. (quickly)
6. She explained the rule ___ the second time. (clearly)
7. Work ___ , and check every line. (carefully)
grammar.answerKey:
1. more slowly  2. the most clearly  3. more carefully  4. more easily  5. the most quickly  6. more clearly  7. more carefully
Wrong on 2 or 5? Three or more, so say the most.
Wrote careful or clear? Those describe the person. The way needs -ly: carefully, clearly.

grammar.title: Have to for a rule, might for a chance
grammar.explanation:
Have to means you cannot avoid it. A rule or a job makes you do it.
Had to is the same thing, yesterday.
Might, may and could mean it is only possible.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
No choice, now:
I have to show my card.
She has to work on Saturday.
Do I have to pay today?
You do not have to pay today.

No choice, in the past:
I had to wait for an hour.
Did you have to pay?

Only possible:
It might rain later.
I may be late.
She could be at the desk.

After have to, use the plain verb:
have to go, has to wait, had to walk

After might, may and could, use the plain verb too:
might go, may wait, could be

Do not have to is not the same as forbid.
It means there is no rule about it.
grammar.workedExample:
A notice says: Members only. Show your card at the desk.
1. Is there a choice? No. The rule says show your card.
2. No choice, so I use have to.
3. I have to show my card at the desk.
4. Now, will the room be free at six? Nobody knows.
5. Not a rule, only possible. I use might, may or could.
6. The room might be free at six.
7. Check: after have to the verb is plain, show, not shows.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to add -s after have to.
No: I have to shows my card.
Yes: I have to show my card.
It is easy to add to after might.
No: It might to rain.
Yes: It might rain.
grammar.memoryTip: Have to: no choice. Might, may, could: only a chance.

8. Is it a rule? ___ I bring a photo?
grammar.answerKey:
1. have to show  2. had to walk  3. might rain  4. has to start  5. might be  6. had to fill  7. do not have to pay  8. Do I have to bring
May and could are also right in 3 and 5.
Wrong on 4? He, she and it take has to.
Wrong on 7? Do not have to means there is no rule. It does not forbid it.

grammar.title: The woman who fixed it: saying exactly which one
grammar.explanation:
Two short sentences about the same person can become one.
Use who for a person and which for a thing.
That works for both.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
A person takes who:
The woman fixed my phone. She works here.
The woman who fixed my phone works here.

A thing takes which:
I lost the card. It opens the door.
I lost the card which opens the door.

That works for a person or a thing:
The person that answered was very helpful.
This is the form that you have to sign.

A place takes where:
This is the room where you wait.

Put who, which or that straight after the noun it points at.
Take out the second he, she or it.
grammar.workedExample:
Two sentences: I met a person. The person gave me the form.
1. Both sentences are about the same person.
2. A person takes who.
3. Cut the second the person and put who in its place.
4. I met the person who gave me the form.
5. Now two sentences about a thing.
6. I lost the card. The card opens the door.
7. A thing takes which or that.
8. I lost the card which opens the door.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to keep the extra he, she or it.
No: The woman who she fixed my phone works here.
Yes: The woman who fixed my phone works here.
It is easy to use which for a person.
No: The man which helped me was kind.
Yes: The man who helped me was kind.
grammar.memoryTip: Who for a person. Which for a thing. That for both. Where for a place.

grammar.answerKey:
1. who  2. which  3. which  4. where  5. who  6. which  7. who  8. where
That is also right in 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7.
Wrong on 4 or 8? A place takes where.
Wrote which for a person? People take who.

teacherNotes.note: Every pattern card shows one item done before its practice, every exercise carries a key with score lines, and every speaking task ends with record, listen back and a short checklist. Speaking 4 is written so one learner says both parts of the conversation; a second person is offered but never needed. If you are helping, listen to the recordings together and point at the checklist rather than correcting mid-sentence.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.sourceFile: Grade 3 Unit 6, Grade 3 Unit 8; Grade 4 Unit 6
teacherNotes.note: Three errors are worth watching for. First, more and -er together: more usefuller. Second, the describing word in place of the -ly word: she works more careful. Third, and the most damaging, reading do not have to as must not. Do not have to means no rule applies; must not means it is not allowed. Pattern 3 states this twice and quiz item 5 tests it directly, because a learner who confuses the two will misread a notice.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.sourceFile: Grade 3 Unit 6, Grade 3 Unit 8; Grade 4 Unit 6
teacherNotes.note: This is the last unit of Stage 4, so it looks back. Practice 6 and quiz items 8 to 12 test Units 1 to 6: the he, she and it forms, the short question on the end, have and has with the past form and yet, be going to, was and were with -ing, and a little with things you cannot count. The assignment asks for one written sentence from an earlier unit as well. A learner who scores 4 or fewer on Practice 6 should redo the pattern cards named in the wrong items before starting Stage 5.

teacherNotes.sourceFile: Grade 3 Unit 6, Grade 3 Unit 8; Grade 4 Unit 6
teacherNotes.note: The notice in Reading 3, the word licence and the rules vocabulary are examples for language practice only. Reading 3 says so in its first line, and the word entries for regulation and licence repeat it. Nothing here describes real rules anywhere, and no task asks the learner for personal papers, status, health or money details. Every task that could touch the learner's own life says plainly that a made-up answer is fine.
